newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FEATURE - Investors moving to develop Ukraine oil reserves.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Investors moving to develop Ukraine oil reserves.

text.p: Ukraine, known more as an oil and gas transit point than as a producer, says its crude oil reserves make it one of the former Soviet Union's last untapped energy frontiers.
A handful of independent and multinational companies are eyeing hydrocarbon reserves here that were last touched in the 1970s.
"They had bigger fields to develop in Siberia," said Nelson Meyers, president of Canada-based Trident (88) Exploration Ltd. "(But) there are a lot of reserves here."

The State Oil and Gas Committee, which says Ukraine's oil could one day wean Kiev from Russian supplies, puts Ukrainian crude oil reserves at 1.05 billion tonnes, with one third of the total in its Black Sea continental shelf.
The level could mean Ukraine has reserves roughly the size of those of Norway or Algeria.

While that is a drop in the ocean compared to Russia's proven reserves of 6.7 trillion tonnes, and the committee's figures are not yet supported by comprehensive Western data, industry executives say Ukraine's cache is worth a look.
"I'm a geologist and was very surprised at the extent of oil deposits. They're numerous," said Mike Monea, president of Canadian independent oil and gas producer Nautilus and Associates.
"The information has never been published in geological circles. They never let it be known."
COUNTRY NEEDS CASH AND KNOW-HOW
Ukraine is largely a novice at tapping hydrocarbons, making it dependent on foreign help.

"Ukraine has lots of oil and gas, it just doesn't have the technology and money," said Rocky Rombs of Canada's Lateral Vector Resources, which is in joint-venture negotiations with Ukrnafta, Kiev's oil exploration monopoly.
Trident, which plans to invest $30 million next year to explore for oil, is one of several independents braving Kiev's red-tape and high taxes.
"The technology that they've been using underestimates what they really have," said Rombs, adding that Lateral Vector planned to use 3-D seismic testing techniques.
In a leading proposal, Shell Oil Company unit Shell Pecten has said it is eyeing a $1 billion gas pipeline and oil drilling deal, including Black Sea shelf reserves.
The arrival of geophysical firms and independent producers could change the energy game in Ukraine, where small oil and gas production levels have declined in recent years.
Ukrainian oil output this year will be flat at 4.2 million tonnes, while natural gas output will slip to 15.2 billion cubic metres from 18.2 billion last year.

Kiev will import 12.3 million tonnes of crude oil and 70 billion cubic metres of natural gas this year, mostly from Russia and Turkmenistan, and had total energy debts of $4.6 billion at the start of this year.
INDEPENDENTS BRAVE RISKS
Some independents, nimble enough to handle the challenges of risky places like Ukraine, are already active.
Rombs said Lateral Vector planned to spend $12 million on exploration in the eastern Sumy region next year.
Carpathian Oil, a joint venture between U.S. Laslo and Ukrnafta, and Kashtan Petroleum, a project grouping Fountain Oil Inc unit UK-RAN Oil Corp and Ukrnafta, are eyeing reserves in Western Ukraine.
Canada's Fountain Oil Inc formed a 45-55 joint venture with Ukranafta in November to further develop the Stynawske field in Western Ukraine.

The two sides also have a joint venture to develop the Lelyaky field in central Ukraine, and Fountain recently announced that it awarded a $1.2 million contract to a Croatian drilling contractor for 12 existing wells on the oilfield.

JFX Oil and Gas Plc has been working in the eastern Poltava region, while U.S. company Marathon Oil Co, a unit of USX-Marathon Group, has been mulling investments of up to $200 million in the Poltava natural gas field.

Canadian independent Epic Energy Inc said in June it had completed its initial test production drilling programme in the Aktash field in Crimea and that it saw "significant oil potential" in the former Soviet republic.
The deals are new for Ukraine, until recently known more as a key transport link between Russian and European oil and gas markets.

Russia sends up to 120 billion cubic metres of gas a year to European customers via Ukraine and about 50 billion cubic metres to Ukraine itself. The Friendship (Druzhba) oil pipeline linking Russia to Eastern Europe runs through Ukraine, and nearly all of Russia's natural gas exports to Europe pass through Ukraine.
TAX BREAKS TO WOO INVESTORS
Kiev, trying to show it is serious about attracting investors, has proposed tax breaks to two joint ventures.
But operating in this country, still suffering from economic collapse and in love with its Soviet-era bureaucratic way of life, is not easy.
"The Ukrainian government needs to get in place a tax regime that will entice foreign companies to come here," said Rombs.

Nautilus and Associates' Monea, whose firm is considering forming an exploration gruop to provide cash and technology in exchange for land and licenses, said the tax regime would have to change before the company considered investing.
"Taxes are very high. We have to crunch numbers to see if it's worth investing millions," he said.
Ukraine, a country of 52 million people, has attracted only about $1.2 billion in foreign investment since independence in 1991 and investors complain of vague laws and bureaucratic stumbling blocks.
Ownership of Black Sea continental shelf resources is unclear.

An international convention gives Ukraine ownership of resources along 200 miles (320 km) of its Black Sea coastline, but uncertainties over interpretation could make tapping the resources as contentious as ownership of Caspian Sea resources.
Kiev is already in a dispute with Romania, a neighbour also bordering the Black Sea, over ownership of tiny Serpent Island, located 25 miles (40 km) from the mouth of the Danube.
Each side, aware of the possibility of rich oil reserves in the area, claims the island, in what could become a test case of how Black Sea continental shelf reserves will be exploited.
Ukraine, not yet experiencing an oil boom, lags behind oil- and gas-rich former Soviet republics like Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan in attracting energy investment dollars.
"It remains to be seen if the total goal of energy self-sufficiency can be achieved," Myers said.
